Manumit

man-yoo-MIT · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To manumit to formally release someone from slavery.

Historical records show the estate chose to manumit several workers after decades of service.

Worked Example

In his final will, the elderly merchant manumitted every person he had once held in bondage.

The will didn't just improve their conditions -- it formally and legally ended their enslavement, which is exactly manumit.

How Manumit Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

free

free: release from slavery or confinement

liberate

liberate: set someone free from restriction

Antonyms

enslave

enslave: force someone into slavery

How Strong Is It? — release → manumit → emancipate

release vs. manumit

release vs. manumit: Releasing someone can mean letting them go from many kinds of restriction; manumit specifically means legally ending their enslavement.

emancipate vs. manumit

emancipate vs. manumit: Manumit describes one person or owner freeing enslaved individuals; this unit's own emancipate describes a broader legal or social liberation, often for an entire group.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of manumit.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — manu

root — manu: hand (Latin (manus))

root — mit

root — mit: to send, release (Latin (mittere))

Put it together

Put it together: Manumit comes from Latin manus ('hand') + mittere ('to send') -- literally 'to send from the hand,' the ancient legal image of releasing someone from an owner's grasp.

Use the root in a new word: transmit

Use the root in a new word: transmit: The same mittere root gives us transmit, 'to send across,' and permit, 'to send through' (that is, to allow).
